Lippe
lip'e
n. (Westphalian county between the Weser and the Teutoburg forest, brought to the Reformed confession by Count Simon the Sixth)
German Lippe, from the river Lippe, a name of Celtic or early Germanic origin; the county took its name from the lords of Lippe.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The county of Lippe lay between the Weser and the Teutoburg forest, and it took the Reformation in the Lutheran form in the middle of the sixteenth century. Count Simon the Sixth, who ruled from 1563, was a learned prince in correspondence with the Reformed theologians of the Rhine, and about the turn of the seventeenth century he carried his county over from the Lutheran to the Reformed confession—the step German historians call a second reformation, by which several princes of the Empire moved their lands from Wittenberg to Heidelberg. In Lippe, as elsewhere, it was easier to decree than to accomplish. The town of Lemgo, the largest in the county, refused: it held to the Augsburg Confession and to its Lutheran ministers, resisted the count's church ordinance, and after a long dispute the two sides came to a written settlement by which Lemgo kept its Lutheran religion inside a Reformed county. Thereafter Lippe was Reformed and Lemgo was not, and both remained so for three hundred years. The dictionary enters Lippe for that outcome, which is more instructive than a clean victory. A prince carried his territory and a single stubborn town would not be carried, and the settlement which admitted the fact was wiser than the decree which had denied it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a confession as a formulary of the articles of faith; conformity as compliance with an established form; and a settlement as an adjustment of differences.

expand to see more

CONFESSION, n. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; a public avowal of belief.

CONFORMITY, n. Compliance with an established form, rule, practice or custom, particularly in religion.

SETTLEMENT, n. The act of settling; adjustment of differences; a final agreement between parties in dispute.

STUBBORN, adj. Unreasonably obstinate; inflexible; not to be moved or persuaded by reasons; hence, persevering.

DECREE, n. [L. decretum.] Judicial decision; an order, edict or law made by a superior as a rule to govern inferiors.

Key Scripture

2Th 2:15 — "Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle."

Rom 13:1 — "Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God."

Tit 1:9 — "Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers."

Jud 1:3 — "Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints."

Modern Corruption

Westphalian county carried from the Lutheran to the Reformed confession about 1600, except for the town of Lemgo, which refused and kept its own.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The genuine question is whether the second reformations were a reform or an imposition, and the dictionary answers it in two parts. The doctrine the Reformed princes adopted was the truer doctrine, and the dictionary holds it—on the Supper, on the second commandment and images, on election. The means were wrong: a confession is a thing a church receives and subscribes, not a thing a prince decrees for his subjects, and where the two are confused the resulting conformity is worth very little.

The principle to recover is in the apostle's word to a congregation rather than to a court: “Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught” (2Th 2:15). Lemgo did exactly that. The dictionary does not agree with what Lemgo was holding, and notes that it held it in the right way—by the town's own conviction, against its prince, at cost—while the rest of the county received the better doctrine in the worse manner.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek paradosis (G3862), that which is handed down; Greek steko (G4739), to stand fast.

expand to see more

Greek steko (G4739) — to stand firm, to stand fast; “stand fast, and hold the traditions”, 2 Thessalonians 2:15.

Greek paradosis (G3862) — that which is handed down, a tradition; 2 Thessalonians 2:15.

Greek exousia (G1849) — authority, delegated power; “there is no power but of God”, Romans 13:1.

Greek antechomai (G472) — to hold fast to; “Holding fast the faithful word”, Titus 1:9.

Greek epagonizomai (G1864) — to contend earnestly for; “earnestly contend for the faith”, Jude 3.

Usage

"“stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught” (2Th 2:15) — the town of Lemgo, against its own count."

"“Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1) — and a confession is not among the things a prince may decree."

"“Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9) — a Reformed county with a Lutheran town in it for three hundred years."
